newsitem.title: SPAIN: IADB weighs direct loan deals with Latam cities.
newsitem.headline: IADB weighs direct loan deals with Latam cities.

text.p: BARCELONA, Spain, March 14, Reuter - The Inter-American Development Bank said on Friday it was actively considering a policy change allowing it to deal directly with Latin American cities applying for loans.

"On the question of financing...we are studying whether we can take the matter one step further, in order to deal on a more direct basis with the municipalities of the 21st century," IADB President Enrique Iglesias told a seminar on Latin American and Caribbean cities in the 21st century.

"One of the things the bank is working on is how we can take steps forward in working with the local authorities -- no decision of the bank has been taken so far, but it is now under consideration," he told reporters later.

Iglesias was speaking ahead of Monday's opening of the IADB's 38th annual meeting. The bank said some 5,000 delegates from 46 member countries have registered to attend the three-day conference in Spain's Catalan capital, Barcelona.

Iglesias declined to offer any estimate of when the bank's board of governors might make a decision, but said the matter was under active consideration for those cities that had the capacity to sustain a certain level of indebtedness.
Mayor after mayor of cities from Brazil to Venezuela pressed the bank to deal with them directly.
"Rio can launch bonds on the international capital markets,...so why can't it have direct loans from the bank for municipal requirements?" said Rio de Janeiro mayor Luiz Paulo Conde.
"The gross domestic product of Rio is four percent of that of Brazil. In Rio the bank can give loans to companies, so why not the municipalities?" he said.
The IABD's private investment arm, the Inter-American Investment Corporation, provides funds to small and medium enterprises, lending some $536 million in the six years to 1995.
The mayor of host city Barcelona, Pasqual Maragall, while not a candidate for IADB lending, added his voice to the request made by his Latin American counterparts.

"If we have an S&P rating or a Moody's rating that is not much worse than that of the sovereign, why not lend money to us directly?" he said, referring to credit rankings from the major U.S. rating agencies.
The IADB normally makes loans to federal and state governments but since its origin in 1959 has not lent to cities or municipalities directly.
The bank is the leading multilateral lender to Latin America. About one-third of the $7 billion it lends to the region each year is targeted at the alleviation of poverty endemic across the region.
